claim: From 1982 to 2024 the Bay of Bengal had more than twice as many cyclones as the Arabian Sea: 120 vs 51 in IMD's annual table (ratio 2.35).

evidence.quote: 1982-2024 (43 yrs): disturbances Bay 277 Arabian 106 | cyclones Bay 120 Arabian 51 ratio 2.35

notes: IMD's own table (CY02 S23, counted by method/count_imd_annual.py). The long record is almost 4:1 (536 vs 139, 1891-2024); the satellite-era 2:1 is used because it is today's picture (CY02 myth M2).

claim: Murasu is a severe cyclonic storm of the Bay of Bengal: on 2 Nov 2026 IMD placed it over the west-central Bay off the south Andhra Pradesh coast.

evidence.quote: over Westcentral Bay of Bengal off south Andhra Pradesh coast

claim: The Arabian Sea is colder than the Bay of Bengal, and IMD says this holds back the formation and strengthening of cyclones there (warm water feeds them).

evidence.quote: the Arabian Sea is relatively colder than Bay of Bengal and
hence inhibits the formation and intensification of the system.

notes: CY02 myth M5: warmer every month (ERSST), but the gap is largest in the monsoon months when few cyclones form, so warmth is one reason, not the whole reason. Script says 'warm water feeds storms', not 'warmth explains the count'.

claim: After the monsoon, a shallow layer of fresh river and rain water caps a deep warm layer in the north Bay, so a cyclone's mixing brings up warm water, not cold, and even the strongest post-monsoon cyclones do not cool the open north Bay.

evidence.quote: a shallow layer of freshwater from river runoff and monsoon rain caps a deep warm layer
even the strongest post-monsoon cyclones do not cool the open north Bay of Bengal
storm-induced mixing is not deep, and it entrains warm subsurface water

notes: Scope: post-monsoon, north Bay. Murasu formed further south (west-central Bay), so the script does not say the lid fed Murasu.

claim: Two of the main reasons surges are disastrous at the Bay's head are shallow coastal water and the convergence (narrowing) of the Bay.
notes: 'Funnel' is our analogy for 'convergence of the Bay' and is labelled an analogy on screen. CY02 C034 measured the narrowing (1,397 km at 16N to 492 km at 21.5N); not spoken here.

claim: A storm surge is an abnormal rise of sea level as the cyclone crosses the coast, and IMD calls surges by far the greatest killers in a cyclone.

evidence.quote: Storm Surge is an abnormal rise of sea level as the cyclone crosses the coast.
The storm surges are by far the greatest killers in a cyclone.

claim: The Bay narrows sharply towards its head: about 1,400 km wide at 16N (Andhra Pradesh coast to the Ayeyarwady coast of Myanmar) but under 500 km at 21.5N (Odisha coast to the Chittagong coast of Bangladesh).

evidence.quote: lat  16.0N: west coast 81.156E (India), east coast 94.224E (Myanmar), width 1397 km
lat  21.5N: west coast 87.101E (India), east coast 91.861E (Bangladesh), width 492 km

method: Natural Earth 1:10m admin-0 (India POV); sea run along the parallel containing 88E; great-circle length along the parallel (haversine, R=6371.0088 km). Script method/bay_width.py.
notes: Map only (ruler lines on the b5 map); not spoken. Natural Earth geometry, our own measurement (CY02 C034).
